newsitem.title: PERU: INTERVIEW-Shell sees Peru natgas potential bonanza.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Shell sees Peru natgas potential bonanza.

text.p: The scope for Shell's huge Camisea gas project could mushroom way beyond early hopes as companies begin to wake up to the potential of Peru's largest foreign investment plan, a top company official said.
Shell is a unit of Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch/Shell group.

Halfway through a two-year license to study the Camisea reserves, the oil giant already sees its work to develop a natural gas market here bearing fruit, Shell's managing director in Peru, Alan Hunt, said in a weekend interview.

The most eye-catching breakthrough is the letter of intent Shell hopes to sign this month with U.S.-based Transpacific Iron-Carbide Corp in a supply deal set to be Camisea's largest contract at 120 million cubic feet of gas per day, Hunt said.

The multinational is also only two months away from "entering its biggest ever (construction) alliance" to build a $1.5 billion gas pipeline, and a Colombian firm is studying a $120 million investment to distribute gas in Lima, he added.

"Camisea has a growth potential that nobody, including the government, could have envisaged even nine months ago," Hunt said. "We are now signing letters of intent, putting money on the table and other guys are spending money on the back of the project."

When the government granted Shell its license in May 1996, President Alberto Fujimori called it the "contract of the century". Shell was set to spend up to $3 billion developing reserves -- estimated to hold 11 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and 600 million barrels of natural gas liquids -- bring the government $6 billion in tax revenue.
But that appears now to be just the beginning.
Shell, operator of the Camisea joint venture with Mobil, began this year's $125 million investment scheme with appraisal drilling and come up with projects not considered in its original plans.
The most novel project was the "exciting possibility" of building a $1 billion ethylene plant that would take 850,000 tonnes per year of ethane from Camisea, Hunt said.

Shell first planned to route its pipeline from the Camisea jungle 300 miles (500 km) over the Andes to the Pacific coast to supply mainly cement firms in Lima and the fish industry in Pisco, 160 miles (250 km) to the south, by the end of 2002.

But Shell was ahead of schedule meaning Lima should receive gas by the end of 2001 and extending the pipeline further south to Marcona or even possibly on to the fast-growing mining areas in southern Peru was not ruled out, Hunt said.

Without these extensions, a scheme to use Camisea's gas in a 300 megawatt power plant -- with the possibility of later doubling its capacity -- meant Shell would likely link up with the government's planned national electricity grid and so indirectly supply energy to the south, Hunt said.
"There is an amazing mushroom of opportunities," he said. "You do not need much imagination to see there could be a breaking of the dam walls."
Realizing Camisea's enormous potential, however, depends on other firms -- like Transpacific -- sinking money into Peru on the back of Shell's investment.

While the Anglo-Dutch firm could vote to go ahead with its Camisea project by year end, Shell was not officially due to make a decision until mid-1998 and this meant many companies were holding off on their potential investment, Hunt said.

"We are saying: 'Don't wait and see. Come and help us make it happen'. Peru might not be AAA risk-rated, but having Shell on the end of the country's major energy resource is about as good as it gets."

He added investors would likely have more faith the project was going ahead in August, when Shell was set to sign a preliminary accord for building the pipeline to the coast. "When we sign that deal the project becomes half-pregnant and from then on keeps getting more pregnant," he said.
Investors could also be confident Fujimori's investor- friendly government would do all it could to make the Camisea project go ahead, according to Hunt.
"The country's potential energy boom is never going to be undermined by the government," he said. "The government has been completely understanding. They deeply want this to happen."
((-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134))
